# 11 — Benchmarks: real chains, real attacks, and where a signing reviewer sits

**Generated by `signing-core/bench/report.py` from `signing-core/bench/results/`. Do not edit by hand.**
Data collected 4–5 October 2026; generated 05 October 2026.

Four questions, each answered from real data rather than from fixtures chosen to pass:

1. Does the reviewer compute exactly what a signer signs, on every chain it claims?
2. What does it say about ordinary traffic, and how often does it cry wolf?
3. Shown the transactions real attacks got people to sign, does it catch them?
4. Of all the money lost in crypto hacks, how much went through the step it guards?

The method for each is described where its results are, and everything can be rerun:
see [How to reproduce](#how-to-reproduce). Where the answer is unflattering it is given
as plainly as where it is not.

## The short version

| | Result |
|---|---|
| Real transactions, 31 chains | Committed to exactly the digest the sender signed: **9,998 of 9,998**. Accepted 100.0% of provable transactions (was 98.0%) |
| Real Safe transactions, 27 chains | Hash equal to Safe's service in **10,851 of 10,851**, and to alloy in all. **13,467 of 13,467** owner signatures and **13,141 of 13,141** signatures accepted on-chain recover to an owner over the hash it computed |
| Real attacks, replayed | Of 13 signer-deception attacks replayed from the chain, the mechanism was named in **9** (was 3) |
| The hack record, 1,293 incidents, $21.07B | **4.3% of incidents and 10.4% of value** went through a deceived signer — the only kind of attack a signing reviewer can stop. Key theft was 51.3% of value and contract bugs 31.9% |
| Speed | A Safe review in 7 µs; 41,324 real Safe reviews a second on one core |
| Robustness | 310,403,474 fuzzing executions across 4 targets, 0 failures. Mutation testing: 98.1% of mutants caught (84.2% before); every survivor is equivalent. |

## 1. Does it compute what the signer actually signs?

A reviewer whose hash is not the hash being signed is worse than none: it gives a
confident answer about something else. So the first measurement checks the digest
against the strongest witness available, the signature itself.

### Plain transactions: 10,493 from 31 chains

Blocks were spread over about two days of each chain's history, ending 2,000 blocks
behind the head, and every transaction in them was kept up to 1,200 per chain. For
each one, alloy rebuilt the unsigned payload from the chain's record, and the payload
was used only if the signature on the chain recovers to the sender over its keccak —
proof that it is byte for byte what the sender's wallet signed. Then clearsign was
given those bytes.

**Before this round of work, 204 of these were refused** (type 0x01: 31, type 0x03: 81, type 0x04: 92) — EIP-2930, EIP-4844
and EIP-7702 transactions, which the decoder did not read. They are now decoded, and the
digest is exact for them too. The 7702 ones matter most: each carries authorizations that
hand an account to code, and they are now CRITICAL instead of refused.

What could not be tested, and why:

- **Chain-specific transaction types (`0x7e`: 293, `0x7b`: 144, `0x6a`: 24, `0x71`: 5).** OP Stack deposits (`0x7e`) and Arbitrum's
  internal transactions (`0x6a`) are made by the system, not signed by anyone. Celo's
  fee-currency transactions (`0x7b`) and zkSync's EIP-712 transactions (`0x71`) are signed
  by people, and clearsign cannot read them: a real gap for users of those two chains.
- **29 transactions on Kaia** whose public API presents Kaia's own transaction types as
  Ethereum legacy ones. Their signed bytes are not Ethereum encodings, so no rebuilt payload
  recovers to the sender, and they were excluded rather than counted.

### Safe transactions: 10,851 from 27 chains

Safes were sampled, not chosen: on each chain, every address that emitted Safe's
`ExecutionSuccess` event in recent blocks was a candidate, and the three busiest plus
seven at random were taken, with up to 100 of their most recent transactions from Safe's
Transaction Service. That gave 248 Safes, 130 of them real multisigs with a threshold of
two or more. Three checks were made on every transaction:

- the hash clearsign computes, against the hash Safe's service published and the hash alloy
  computes;
- every owner signature that is an ordinary ECDSA signature, recovered over clearsign's hash;
- for the 10,621 transactions already executed, the packed signatures the Safe contract itself
  accepted on-chain, recovered the same way. If clearsign's hash were wrong, they would
  recover to strangers.

| **All** | **10,851** | **248** | **10,851/10,851** | **10,851/10,851** | **13,467/13,467** | **13,141/13,141** | **1,978** | **577** | **7,207** | **1,089** |

The previous live comparison covered 238 transactions on Ethereum alone ([09](09-against-real-transactions.md)).
This one covers every network the application offers except Sepolia, whose log endpoint
refused the discovery queries, and sixteen more. Two things it found are worth knowing:

- **A Safe's domain can change during its life.** One Linea Safe signed its first 4 transactions under
  the v1.1.x domain and every later one under v1.3.0+, because it was upgraded. A tool that
  takes the version from the Safe's *current* state computes the wrong hash for its history.
  clearsign settles the domain from the hash the file carries, and got all of them right; the
  benchmark's own first draft made exactly that mistake, which is how it was found. Each
  transaction's domain is now settled by the owners' own signatures before anything is compared.
- **Safe's service sometimes writes `null` for a zero address.** 1 executed Unichain transaction
  gave `gasToken` and `refundReceiver` as `null`, and the reader refused it. It is now accepted
  only when the file's own hash proves the zero-address reading, and the review says so.

## 2. What it says about ordinary traffic

The same corpora, read for what the reviewer told the person signing.

| | Clear | Warning | BLIND | CRITICAL |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Real transactions (9,998 accepted) | 16.3% | 1.7% | 78.9% | 3.1% |
| Real Safe transactions (10,851) | 18.2% | 5.3% | 66.4% | 10.0% |
| Safe transactions from real multisigs only (5,122) | 26.9% | 7.1% | 56.4% | 9.6% |

**BLIND is the number to look at.** It is the share of real activity the reviewer cannot
read: swaps, staking, bridging, account-abstraction bundles and every other function outside
its verified set. It refuses those rather than guessing, which is the design, but it means
that on 56% of what real multisigs sign, its answer is "I cannot tell you what this does."
That is the honest size of the gap between this tool and a reviewer that understands DeFi.

**CRITICAL in ordinary traffic is mostly correct.** On Safes it is made of:

| Finding | Safe transactions | before this work |
|---|---:|---:|
| `UNLIMITED_APPROVAL` | 506 | 504 |
| `SAFE_DELEGATECALL` | 271 | 271 |
| `SAFE_OWNER_CHANGE` | 270 | 270 |
| `APPROVAL_FOR_ALL` | 242 | 0 |
| `PROXY_UPGRADE` | 73 | 0 |
| `ROLE_GRANT` | 69 | 0 |
| `SAFE_THRESHOLD_CHANGE` | 35 | 35 |
| `SAFE_MODULE_CHANGE` | 32 | 32 |
| `OWNERSHIP_TRANSFER` | 8 | 0 |

Unlimited approvals, owner changes, upgrades and role grants are exactly what a signer
should confirm one by one, and they are what the attacks in section 3 used. The exception is
`SAFE_DELEGATECALL`: most of those are Safe's own helper contracts (SignMessageLib,
SafeMigration) called the way they are meant to be. Pinning those by address and chain, as
MultiSend already is, would make that warning more specific; see section 8.

**164 real transactions called a known function with non-canonical arguments** — almost all a
`transfer` with extra bytes appended — and were marked CRITICAL. Two applications on Plasma
and Gnosis account for most; several others carried kilobytes of addresses behind the
`transfer` selector, the shape of an address-poisoning dispatcher dressed up as a transfer.
Refusing to call those transfers is the reviewer working as intended.

## 3. Real attacks, replayed

The transactions real attacks got people to sign were fetched from the chain and rebuilt
without trusting any service. A Safe attack was rebuilt from the `execTransaction` calldata
the chain recorded, decoded by alloy; its nonce and domain, which are not in the calldata,
were found by search — the right ones reproduce the hash the Safe contract itself emitted —
and the owners' signatures then had to recover over that hash. A transaction signed by a
person had to recover to that person. Only then was it shown to the reviewer, once built from
the code before this work (commit `3258e8d3`) and once from the code after.

| Incident | Chain | Lost | What the victim signed | Before | After |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Bybit | Ethereum | $1.40B | Safe `DELEGATECALL` to attacker code, shown as a token transfer | **DO NOT SIGN** — `SAFE_DELEGATECALL` | **DO NOT SIGN** — `SAFE_DELEGATECALL` |
| WazirX | Ethereum | $234.9M | Safe `DELEGATECALL` replacing the implementation, shown as GALA/USDT transfers | **DO NOT SIGN** — `SAFE_DELEGATECALL` | **DO NOT SIGN** — `SAFE_DELEGATECALL` |
| Radiant Capital (Arbitrum) | Arbitrum | $50.0M | `transferOwnership` of the protocol's address provider to the attacker | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `OWNERSHIP_TRANSFER` |
| Radiant Capital (BNB Chain) | BNB Chain |  | The same ownership transfer on BNB Chain | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `OWNERSHIP_TRANSFER` |
| Uniswap V3 LP phishing | Ethereum | $8.0M | `setApprovalForAll` on Uniswap V3 positions to the phisher | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `APPROVAL_FOR_ALL` |
| Uniswap V3 LP phishing | Ethereum |  | `setApprovalForAll` on Uniswap V3 positions to the phisher | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `APPROVAL_FOR_ALL` |
| Badger DAO | Ethereum | $120.0M | Unlimited `increaseAllowance` to the attacker, from an injected script | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `UNLIMITED_APPROVAL` |
| Badger DAO | Ethereum |  | Unlimited `increaseAllowance` to the attacker, from an injected script | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `UNLIMITED_APPROVAL` |
| Nexus Mutual founder | Ethereum | $8.0M | A plain transfer of 370,000 NXM to the attacker, behind a tampered MetaMask | Nothing flagged | Nothing flagged |
| POAP founder (listed as Rocket Pool) | Ethereum | $3.8M | A bounded `approve` of RPL to a drainer | Warning — `TOKEN_APPROVAL` | Warning — `TOKEN_APPROVAL` |
| JayPegs Automart (SushiSwap MISO) | Ethereum | $3.1M | MISO `createMarket` with the attacker's address injected | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded |
| MM Finance (Cronos) | Cronos | $2.0M | `approve` to a fake router injected by DNS hijack, then a swap through it | **DO NOT SIGN** — `UNLIMITED_APPROVAL` | **DO NOT SIGN** — `UNLIMITED_APPROVAL` |
| MM Finance (Cronos) | Cronos |  | `approve` to a fake router injected by DNS hijack, then a swap through it | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded |
| KlaySwap (BGP hijack) | Kaia | $1.9M | `approve` to a fake factory, from a BGP-hijacked script | Not reviewable | Not reviewable |
| EIP-7702 batch phishing (Ethereum) | Ethereum | $147K | The victim's own 7702 account running a batch of approvals | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `UNLIMITED_APPROVAL` |
| EIP-7702 batch phishing (Base) | Base | $1.5M | The same, on Base | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded | **DO NOT SIGN** — `APPROVAL_FOR_ALL` |

**The mechanism was named in 9 of these 13 incidents, up from 3.** What changed is
specificity, not the verdict: before, most of these already ended in DO NOT SIGN, but only
because the reviewer could not decode them — the same answer it gives to
56% of ordinary multisig traffic. A warning that fires on most of
what you sign stops being read. Radiant's signers would have seen "unknown function"; they
now see that they are handing ownership of the protocol to an address they do not control.

The rest, plainly:

- **Nexus Mutual (2020)**: a tampered MetaMask showed the founder one thing and his Ledger signed
  a plain transfer of 370,000 NXM to the attacker. clearsign shows that transfer and its
  recipient faithfully — which is the whole defence against a tampered interface — but a token
  transfer is not itself alarming, so nothing is flagged. Only a person comparing the screen
  with their intent catches this one.
- **POAP's founder (2023)**: a bounded `approve` to a drainer gets a WARNING naming the spender,
  not a refusal: a bounded approval is an ordinary thing to sign.
- **JayPegs / SushiSwap MISO (2021)**: `createMarket` with the attacker's address injected is
  outside the verified set, so it is BLIND — refused, but not explained.
- **KlaySwap (2022)**: Kaia's native transaction format, which clearsign does not read.

**Attacks no reviewer that reads bytes can catch.** In these the transaction said exactly what
it did, and the victim was wrong about who they were paying:

| Incident | What happened | What clearsign said |
|---|---|---|
| SUPERFORTUNE AI | A Safe batch paying a look-alike of the airdrop contract's address | Warning — `SAFE_MULTISEND_BATCH` |
| Florence Finance | A Safe USDC transfer to an address-poisoning look-alike | Nothing flagged |
| Ionic Protocol | An admin Safe listing a counterfeit token as collateral | DO NOT SIGN — BLIND, not decoded |
| Fake GIWA bridge | ETH deposited into a fake bridge portal | Nothing flagged |
| Phantom Galaxies | A 0.1 ETH "mint fee" paid straight to a scammer | Nothing flagged |
| EigenLayer (OTC address swap) | A Safe batch in which one recipient had been swapped by email | Warning — `SAFE_MULTISEND_BATCH` |
| CoinDash ICO | ETH sent to the address that replaced the ICO address on a hacked site | Nothing flagged |

An address-poisoning victim sees the attacker's address in full on clearsign's screen. It
cannot know that the address is not the one they meant. Defences against this class live
elsewhere: address books, allowlists, and confirming a recipient over a second channel.

**Not covered at all**, because the victims signed something clearsign does not read: Drift
(Solana, 2026, about $295M) and SwissBorg (Solana, 2025, $41.5M), both signers deceived into
approving disguised transactions; DMM Bitcoin (Bitcoin, 2024, $305M); OpenSea's 2022 order
phishing (`personal_sign`); Monkey Kingdom (Solana).

## 4. Where a signing reviewer sits in the hack record

DeFiLlama's hack list holds 1,293 incidents from 2011 to October 2026, totalling
$21.07B. Its labels say what kind of incident each was, not whether a person was
deceived into signing — "private key compromised" covers both a stolen key and a tricked
signer. So every incident of $1M or more in the ambiguous categories (key compromise, social
engineering, frontend and infrastructure, access control, governance) was researched one by
one from post-mortems, security firms' write-ups and the chain itself: 319 incidents, of which
16 turned out to have reached the money through a deceived signer. The rest were classified
by written rules from DeFiLlama's own technique label; the rules are in `bench/landscape.py`
and the research, with its sources, in `bench/corpus/hacks/`.

| How the attack reached the money | Incidents | Value | Share of value |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Key theft — the attacker had the keys and signed for itself | 245 | $10.81B | 51.3% |
| Contract or protocol bug — nobody signed anything | 903 | $6.72B | 31.9% |
| **Multisig owners deceived into signing** | 7 | $2.02B | 9.6% |
| Insider or rug pull | 51 | $459.7M | 2.2% |
| Deceived about the recipient (address poisoning, impersonation) | 10 | $349.2M | 1.7% |
| Unknown | 9 | $287.3M | 1.4% |
| Governance attack | 20 | $255.0M | 1.2% |
| **A person deceived into signing** | 48 | $162.0M | 0.8% |

**A signing reviewer is on the path of 4.3% of incidents and 10.4% of the value lost.**
In formats clearsign reads, 8.8%. That is the ceiling for any tool that works at the moment
of signing, however good. Another 1.7% was lost by people deceived about who they were paying,
which a reviewer of bytes can show but cannot judge. The rest — most of the money — was taken
by people who already held the keys, or from contracts nobody had to sign anything to exploit.

The share has not been constant:

| Year | Lost | Through a deceived signer | Key theft | Contract bugs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2018 | $1.12B | $0 (0.0%) | 82.9% | 1.9% |
| 2019 | $277.3M | $0 (0.0%) | 75.9% | 0.3% |
| 2020 | $3.98B | $8.3M (0.2%) | 95.8% | 3.7% |
| 2021 | $2.87B | $124.4M (4.3%) | 28.6% | 59.2% |
| 2022 | $3.63B | $16.8M (0.5%) | 42.5% | 51.2% |
| 2023 | $1.63B | $5.2M (0.3%) | 59.7% | 35.6% |
| 2024 | $1.67B | $286.3M (17.1%) | 35.8% | 21.7% |
| 2025 | $2.72B | $1.44B (53.1%) | 19.7% | 24.5% |
| 2026 | $2.24B | $299.8M (13.4%) | 31.7% | 50.9% |

The $931.8M lost before 2018 is left out of the table, none of it through a deceived signer.

Before 2024 almost nothing reached the money this way. In 2025 more than half did — Bybit
alone — and the industry's own reports agree on the direction: TRM attributes 76% of 2025's
stolen funds to infrastructure attacks and 12% to code exploits; Chainalysis puts private-key
compromises at 43.8% of 2024's. Neither separates a stolen key from a deceived signer, which
is why the incidents were researched here one by one.

**DeFiLlama's list leaves out most retail theft.** Scam Sniffer counts wallet-drainer losses
of $494M from 332,000 victims in 2024 and $83.85M from 106,106 in 2025. Almost all of that is
signing deception, and it is the part clearsign can now read: of 2024's large drains, Scam
Sniffer attributes 56.7% to permit signatures, 31.9% to one DSProxy `setOwner`, and 3.5% to
`increaseAllowance`; in 2025, Permit and Permit2 were 38% of large drains, with EIP-7702
batches, `approve`, `transfer` and `setApprovalForAll` behind. Permits, Permit2, `setOwner`,
`increaseAllowance`, `setApprovalForAll` and 7702 batches are now decoded, and flagged
CRITICAL by name when they grant unlimited or ownership-level control; a bounded approval
draws a warning, and a plain `transfer` is shown faithfully but not flagged. Typed data is
read by the command-line tool, not yet by the window. Sources and dates are in
`bench/corpus/hacks/loss-landscape-2026-10-05.md`.

## 5. Speed and size

One core of an Apple M5 (10 logical cores, macos/aarch64), release build. Each figure is a
complete review: parse, decode, judge, hash and render the text a signer reads. Each timing is the median of three runs.

| Scenario | Input | Median | p99 | Reviews a second | Memory allocated | Peak held |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| EIP-1559 native transfer | 51 B | 4.2 µs | 5.5 µs | 237,238 | 5,249 B | 2,950 B |
| EIP-1559 ERC-20 transfer | 113 B | 5.2 µs | 11.6 µs | 185,622 | 11,529 B | 6,880 B |
| EIP-1559 unlimited ERC-20 approval | 113 B | 5.2 µs | 6.8 µs | 192,720 | 11,922 B | 6,918 B |
| EIP-1559 with 128 KiB of calldata to an unknown function | 131,125 B | 266.4 µs | 290.5 µs | 3,725 | 140,261 B | 133,052 B |
| Bybit's Safe record: strict JSON read, domain settled from the hash, review, render | 679 B | 12.6 µs | 16.0 µs | 79,605 | 15,243 B | 7,146 B |
| Bybit's Safe transaction: review and render (v1.1.x domain) | 68 B | 7.0 µs | 25.4 µs | 119,868 | 12,547 B | 7,078 B |
| Safe transaction hash alone | 68 B | 1.3 µs | 1.7 µs | 754,414 | 0 B | 0 B |
| Safe MultiSend batch of 32 ERC-20 transfers (all shown) | 4,964 B | 90.1 µs | 104.2 µs | 11,123 | 118,318 B | 60,657 B |
| Safe MultiSend batch of 1,024 calls, the most it will parse | 156,740 B | 2339.2 µs | 2450.0 µs | 427 | 2,764,299 B | 111,573 B |

Over the real corpora: 10,851 Safe transactions in 263 ms (41,324 a second), and 10,019 plain transactions in 63 ms (159,099 a second).
The command-line tool, started fresh for each review of the Bybit record, takes 2.3 ms
end to end (median of 1,800 runs, measured while the machine was in use). The binary is 949,568 bytes; the WebAssembly reviewer the
window embeds is 275,967 bytes.

The signer image is held to tighter limits than this table: it takes requests of at most 64 KiB
and serves each from a 4 MiB arena that never frees, so what counts is everything one review
allocates, not what it holds at once. Of the largest requests that fit —
a malformed transaction filling the request, a plan with every step full, a request-sized multicall of transferOwnership calls, a request-sized multicall of acceptOwnership calls, a MultiSend batch of 32 calls carrying 1,800 bytes each —
the most expensive is a malformed transaction filling the request, at 1,572,768 bytes in total: under the 2 MiB alarm
`crates/clearsign-ffi/tests/arena_budget.rs` enforces, and inside the arena. (The 1,024-call batch
above is larger than any request the signer accepts; it is there to time the desktop tools.)

## 6. Robustness

**Fuzzing, 45 minutes per target on 5 Oct 2026**, on the targets the new code runs through:

| Target | Executions | Coverage edges | Failures |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `tx_bytes` | 104,341,332 | 1167 | 0 |
| `typed_data` | 71,702,543 | 3273 | 0 |
| `calldata` | 22,779,961 | 1350 | 0 |
| `safe_tx` | 16,823,943 | 924 | 0 |

**Again on the final code**, after a review of the new decoders led to five more fixes, 8 minutes per target:

| Target | Executions | Coverage edges | Failures |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `tx_bytes` | 38,281,587 | 1180 | 0 |
| `typed_data` | 21,179,816 | 3357 | 0 |
| `calldata` | 8,386,938 | 1549 | 0 |
| `safe_tx` | 6,200,358 | 988 | 0 |
| `typed_data` (inputs up to 256 KiB, for 10 minutes) | 20,706,996 | 3399 | 0 |

**Mutation testing** (`cargo mutants -p clearsign`, with every test in the workspace): the decoder as it was before this work had 223 mutants caught and 42 missed, a score of 84.2% (12 more timed out and 55 did not compile). After the new decoders and the tests written for the survivors: 617 caught and 12 missed of 718, 98.1% (2 timed out, 87 did not compile). Each of the 12 survivors was examined and is equivalent: no input tells it from the original, so no test can kill it. They are listed with the reason for each in `crates/clearsign/tests/mutation_gaps.rs`.

The JSON readers (`cargo mutants -p clearsign-safe-json`), which take Safe records and typed-data requests from files nobody vouches for: 43 caught and 5 missed of 63, 89.6% (15 did not compile). The survivors are equivalent too; `crates/clearsign-safe-json/tests/strict_input.rs` says why for each.

Differential tests against alloy, an independent and widely used Rust implementation, cover
everything added in this round: 2,000 random cases each for EIP-2930, EIP-4844 and EIP-7702
transactions, the administration and permission calls, multicall, and a never-more-permissive
property on mutated calldata; and 5,000 random EIP-712 documents — nested structs, arrays and
every atomic type — hashed by both. Two bugs planted in the EIP-712 code (dropping dependent
types from the type hash; skipping sign extension of negative integers) were each caught at
once, then removed.

Real typed-data signatures: 258 permits submitted on Ethereum (erc2612: 33, permit2_batch: 2, permit2_single: 223)
were rebuilt from their calldata and hashed by clearsign, and every signature recovered to its
owner. Of those, 227 granted an unlimited allowance and would have been CRITICAL; 31 were bounded.

## 7. What this does not show

- **It is not an audit.** The code added in this round — the new decoders and the EIP-712
  reviewer — was written and tested with AI assistance and has not been read by an independent
  human reviewer. That is still the gate before real funds.
- **The corpora are samples.** The busiest Safes on a chain are often automation with a
  threshold of one, which is why multisig-only figures are given separately. Two days of blocks
  is not a year of them.
- **The attack replay is small.** 13 signer-deception incidents with public, provable
  transactions. Many attacks never publish theirs, and retail drains are represented by classes
  of payload rather than by every victim.
- **The landscape is a classification, with judgement in it.** The research for each incident
  is published with its sources so the judgements can be checked, and DeFiLlama's own figures
  are used for amounts even where other sources differ.
- **Performance is one machine.** Medians are steady from run to run; the p99 column moves with
  whatever else the machine is doing, and is a ceiling seen once rather than a guarantee.
- **Typed data is reviewed, not signed,** and only from the command line: the window still reads
  Safe transactions only, and the signer does not sign typed data.

## 8. What is still open

In rough order of what the measurements say matters:

- **Independent human review** of the code added in this round, and of everything since the
  September review. Nothing here substitutes for it.
- **Typed data in the window, and signing bound to that review.** Permit and Permit2 signatures
  were the largest single class of retail drains in 2024 and 2025, and today only the command
  line reads them.
- **Solana and Bitcoin.** Drift (about $295M), SwissBorg ($41.5M) and DMM Bitcoin ($305M) were
  on the signing path and in formats clearsign does not read.
- **Safe's own helper contracts** — SignMessageLib, SafeMigration, SafeToL2Migration — pinned by
  address and chain as MultiSend is, so their DELEGATECALLs are named rather than treated as
  unknown code.
- **Celo `0x7b` and zkSync `0x71` transactions**, which people sign and clearsign cannot read.
- **The BLIND share.** More than half of what real multisigs sign is outside the verified set.
  Protocol readers (Uniswap, Aave, Lido, bridges) are outside v1's scope; which, if any, belong
  in it is part of the scope sign-off.
- **Permit severity.** 88% of real permits grant an unlimited allowance, so a
  permit review is CRITICAL most of the time. That follows the rule for approvals, and it may
  also teach people to click through. The data makes the question concrete; it does not answer it.
- **Typed-data structures beyond permits**, such as Seaport and UniswapX orders, are shown but BLIND.
- **Hardware, verified boot and code signing**, unchanged by this work.

## How to reproduce

```sh
cd signing-core/bench
python3 collect/safe_corpus.py       # Safe transactions from every chain in collect/chains.py
python3 collect/evm_corpus.py        # transactions from sampled blocks on the same chains
python3 collect/attack_corpus.py     # the attack transactions, from the chain
python3 collect/permit_corpus.py     # permits submitted on Ethereum
cargo run --release --bin verify-evm
cargo run --release --bin verify-safe
cargo run --release --bin detect
cargo run --release --bin verify-permits
cargo run --release --bin perf
python3 landscape.py && python3 report.py
```

The corpora used for this document are committed under `bench/corpus/`, so everything above
can be rerun offline; collecting afresh samples newer blocks and will give similar, not
identical, numbers.
